John Kenneth Galbraith. A twentieth century American economist and prolific public intellectual who challenged both laissez-faire economics and crude Keynesianism, arguing that large corporations and technocracies dominate modern capitalist economies, not competitive markets.

In his 1958 book The Affluent Society, Galbraith argued something scandalous: that demand is not independent and autonomous, as classical economics assumed. Advertising and consumerism drive demand in rich nations. Corporations create wants. Consumers do not arrive at preferences through careful consideration of their needs. Marketing convinces them to buy what corporations want to sell. This undermined the classical assumption that the consumer is sovereign and knows what he wants.

He introduced the concept of the technostructure. Large corporations are not controlled by shareholders. They are controlled by the layer of managers, engineers, and experts who actually run the operations. These technocrats have their own interests and goals, which may diverge from shareholder profit maximization. This insight led to later work on corporate behavior and institutional analysis.

He argued that large firms exercise market power. They are not price-takers, passively accepting the price the market dictates. They have oligopolistic power to influence prices and quantities. Competition is an ideal of small firms in textbooks, not the reality of modern capitalism.

Galbraith was skeptical of growth as a measure of success. He famously criticized private affluence and public squalor. Wealthy individuals living in elegant homes while infrastructure crumbles and schools go unfunded. Economic growth that enriches the private sector while starving public goods is not genuine progress.

He had a distinguished career beyond economics. He served as U.S. ambassador to India from 1961 to 1963 under President Kennedy and worked as an economic policy advisor. He lived to ninety-seven and remained a prolific writer and television personality, translating economic ideas into accessible language for general audiences. He ideologically opposed Milton Friedman and the free-market gospel Friedman championed. He shared intellectual roots with Thorstein Veblen and his critique of conspicuous consumption and institutional irrationality. And while he shared Marx's skepticism about capitalist harmony, Galbraith was no revolutionary.
